title: OnPrem DNS Namespace Convergence and NAT Surge Scenarios
summary: Working-draft playbook for migrating multiple on-prem/private resolvers to a converged namespace and for handling NAT port surge risk during rollout. Includes Terraform module notes, staging/checklist, test plan, and rollback considerations.
content:
Context and motivation:
- Problem: multiple legacy resolvers and split-horizon configurations cause slow lookups, inconsistent service discovery, and a fragile operator model for private deployments.
- Secondary risk: changes to resolver topology and egress (NAT) can produce ephemeral port exhaustion during high-concurrency inference bursts (large batch jobs, autoscale spin-ups).
- Goal: converge to a single resolver profile per VPC (primary + hot-standby), simplify zone delegation, and introduce a staged ingress/egress policy rollout that mitigates NAT port surge risk.

Audience:
- SREs and infra engineers running Private/VPC installations, solutions engineers onboarding customers, platform engineers who maintain terraform modules.

Non-goals:
- Replacing customer-managed authoritative DNS systems. This is purely about resolver/forwarder topology and the cluster-level split-horizon behavior.

High-level plan (phases):
1) Inventory & baseline (2 weeks)
   - Discover all resolvers, forwarders, and split-horizon rules (k8s kube-dns, forwarders on the edge, on-prem DNS appliances).
   - Measure TTLs, NXDOMAIN patterns, and p95 lookup latencies (metric: resolver.lookup.latency by zone).
   - Run NAT-capacity simulation with synthetic clients to estimate ephemeral port usage.
2) Consolidation pilot (1 week)
   - Create single resolver profile in staging VPC, wire a test namespace (serving-dev.*) to it via stub-forward.
   - Deploy probe checks: dig +short, ndots/timeout regression checks.
3) Controlled rollout with NAT mitigation (2–4 weeks)
   - Use canary ingress policy + egress NAT pool expansion (see details below).
   - Monitor ephemeral-port-utilization, tcp_retransmit, and application-level failures.
4) Full migration & pruning (1 week)
   - Remove old forwarders, shrink ttl for failover, update Terraform state to reflect new resolver module inputs.

Detailed items
A) Inventory checklist (commands and datums to gather)
- list resolver endpoints (k8s: kubectl -n kube-system get svc coredns -o wide; on edge: /etc/resolv.conf, systemd-resolved config)
- capture zone delegation records (BIND zones, PowerDNS exports, cloud DNS exports)
- capture firewall rules that affect DNS and egress (iptables -L -n; cloud: aws ec2 describe-network-acls)
- run per-node ephemeral port snapshot: ss -s and /proc/net/nf_conntrack counts
- run synthetic lookup suite: script that 1) queries internal service names 2) queries external names to measure ratio of external lookups

B) NAT surge scenarios and mitigations
- Typical failure mode: many short-lived outbound TCP connections to model registries, telemetry collectors, or control plane during scale-up; each consumes an ephemeral port -> port exhaustion.
- Mitigation options:
  1) NAT port pool expansion: increase number of NAT gateways / SNAT IPs.
  2) Connection reuse: encourage long-lived keep-alive for outbound connections or sidecar connection pools.
  3) Proxy egress: funnel outbound through shared egress proxies (saves ports by multiplexing).
  4) Throttle concurrency during ramp-ups via admission controller or rollout sequencer.
- Staging recipe: when moving resolver topology, schedule canary so that only 5% of nodes switch resolver at a time; measure port usage delta and rollback if port utilization increases > 15% over baseline.

C) Ingress / Firewall rule staging pattern
- Principle: apply least-privilege but stage from permissive -> restricted instead of restriction flips (too risky).
- Staging steps:
  1) Create new intended policy as ALLOW alongside existing broad ALLOW.
  2) Enable alerting for denied-but-allowed equivalence: compare flows matched by old policy vs new policy.
  3) Move small set of namespaces/workloads to new policy via admission-label injection.
  4) Once stable for 48–72h, flip route table and prune old policy.
- Example Kubernetes NetworkPolicy template (for primer):
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-internal-to-redis
    namespace: infra-data
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        role: redis
    ingress:
      - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              stage: backend
        ports:
          - protocol: TCP
            port: 6379

D) Terraform module notes (rdw_dns and rdw_egress helper modules)
- New vars to add to rdw_dns module:
  - var: resolver_profiles (list) => defines primary and fallback IPs, healthcheck endpoint, and ttl_override.
  - var: zone_forwarding_rules (map) => zone -> forwarder IPs, to support selective split-horizon migration.
- State migration: prefer resource replacement with import where possible. Avoid changing resource IDs for NAT gateway attachments in the same apply.
- Example snippet (informal):
  module "rdw_dns" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/rdw-infra/terraform-modules.git//rdw_dns?ref=main"
    resolver_profiles = [{ name = "primary", ips = ["10.0.12.5"] , health = "/health" }]
    zone_forwarding_rules = { "private.rdw.local" = ["10.0.12.6"] }
  }
- Terraform considerations:
  - Keep forwarder IPs as external data sources (dns_forwarder_ips) so changes don't force resource recreation unless intentional.
  - Add lifecycle ignore_changes for ephemeral NAT EIP attachments until we shrink pools in final step.

E) Canary testing and observability signals
- Synthetics:
  - resolver-correctness: run named queries for internal services, expect stable A/AAAA + SRV.
  - egress-port-telemetry: count ephemeral ports in use per-node and publish to metrics exporter.
- Traces & logs:
  - instrument resolver health checks with tags: resolver.profile, resolver.node, deployment-stage.
  - log mismatch events where service A resolves to different IPs across resolvers for > 5m window.
- Alerting thresholds (suggested):
  - resolver.lookup.latency.p95 > baseline * 1.5 -> warn
  - ephemeral_ports_utilization > 70% -> page oncall
  - failed_kv_cache_lookups > 5% -> investigate DNS TTL/forwarder reachability

F) Rollback plan (fast & safe)
- Fast rollback: re-point kubelet/resolv.conf or stub-forwarder to previous resolver IP set (automate via tag-based config map).
- If NAT surge observed: rehydrate old NAT pool (bring additional SNAT IPs online) and throttle new deployments until ports free.
- Postmortem checklist: capture tcpdump traces from border egress nodes, dump conntrack, collect kube events for same time window.

G) Testing matrix (minimal acceptance tests)
- Functional: internal service name resolution before/after migration, NXDOMAIN behavior consistent, SRV record correctness.
- Load: simulate 10k small connections across nodes, watch ephemeral port use and packet drops.
- Failure injection: drop resolver UDP packets to primary; ensure fallback is within 1s and no 5xx spikes in API.

H) Open questions / decisions needed
- Do we want to support per-namespace resolver overrides permanently or strictly per-VPC? (ops tradeoffs)
- What telemetry retention is sufficient for post-migration debugging (48h vs 7d)?
- Should sidecar egress proxy be mandatory for new deployments to limit ephemeral port usage?

I) Next actions (owner and ETA)
- Asha: run inventory script and produce resolver map (ETA 2024-11-27).
- Liam: prototype egress-proxy image and connection-pooling settings (ETA 2024-12-05).
- Maya: add resolver_profiles var to rdw_dns TF module and open draft PR (ETA 2024-12-10).

Notes to self / rough TODOs (scratch)
- build synthetic port-surge test harness (k6 + small TCP client)
- add exporter metric for conntrack size per node
- reconvene with solutions-eng to align customer migration windows

Appendix: quick commands
- Check which resolver a container sees:
  kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
  kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- dig +short service.private.rdw.local @<resolver-ip>
- Snapshot conntrack and ephemeral usage:
  sudo conntrack -S | head -n 50
  ss -tan state established | wc -l

End of draft.

(Work-in-progress; contains TODOs and rough cut Terraform notes. This doc will be converted to a more formal runbook after pilot.)
